description: 🚀 Building a strong team for NASA Space Apps 2026! We’re working on identifying Earth locations that can serve as analogs for future Moon and Mars missions using NASA data, AI/ML, geospatial analysis, and visualization. We’re looking for passionate teammates skilled in AI/ML, GIS, data analysis, web development, design, or storytelling who want to build something ambitious, impactful, and truly space-focused. 🌍🌙🔴
summary:
ELSEWHERE - Exploring other worlds starts with understanding our own.

We developed ELSEWHERE, a web app that finds places on Earth whose terrain resembles any place on the
Moon or Mars, addressing the challenge "Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base
Locations and Mars."

Before astronauts and rovers explore the Moon or Mars, they train on Earth, and training on the wrong
kind of ground can hide problems that appear only on the real surface. In ELSEWHERE, a user picks any
spot on a 3D Moon or Mars globe. The app measures that 20 x 20 km area from NASA elevation data
(slopes, relief and roughness) and searches over a million areas of Earth's land for the closest match
in under a second.

For each match it shows real satellite images of both places, a 3D view of both terrains, and what is
similar and what is different, including NASA climate data and the conditions Earth cannot copy, such
as lower gravity.

This helps mission teams find realistic, lesser-known training grounds quickly and understand each
one's limits.
details:
WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- One method for three worlds: Earth, Mars and the Moon are measured with exactly the same 20 km,

1000 m terrain fingerprint, so any site on the Moon or Mars can be compared with any place on Earth.

- Pin anywhere, not a fixed list: users can explore any crater, valley or plain, not only famous sites,

and most results fall outside the well-known analog areas.

- "What is similar, how similar, what is different" in one view: instead of a single score, each result

shows where the analog holds (terrain, sometimes dryness) and where it breaks (climate, gravity,

atmosphere, radiation).

- Explainable without machine learning: no labelled analog pairs exist, so instead of a black box we

use a fixed distance whose every part can be read and adjusted by the user.

- Storytelling for everyone: a cartoon astronaut jumps to the chosen world, a "what experiment will you

run?" question frames the search, and both terrains appear as 3D blocks built from the real elevation -

making planetary science approachable without hiding the numbers.

FACTORS OUR TEAM CONSIDERED

- Scientific honesty: the index is a heuristic, not a probability; we never claim a "first discovery";

measured values, computed scores, context data and AI text are kept clearly separate.

- Fair comparison: identical grid, window size and metrics on all three bodies, each projected on its

own figure; the same vertical exaggeration for both 3D terrains.

- Data quality: we compared 1 km and 30 m Earth data and disclose the ~20% roughness bias; we reject

windows with missing data or likely water; we flag climate values that are unreliable in mountains.

- Earth's limits: gravity, vacuum or thin CO2 air, and radiation cannot be reproduced, and the app says so.

- Reproducibility: open NASA data, SHA-256 records for every file, automated tests, and a deterministic

decision record.

- Accessibility and performance: keyboard navigation, reduced-motion support, sound off by default,

works on phones; the global search runs in under half a second.

- Responsible AI: the optional AI chat only explains server-computed evidence and never produces

scores; AI-assisted work is disclosed.
